title: POC weekly caching sync - Aperture Labs
summary: Weekly POC sync to review prefix/KV cache hit rates, discuss prompt reuse strategy, surface anomalies (low hit rates on personalization flows), and agree next steps: run targeted benchmark with canonicalization changes, adjust TTLs, and share detailed logs and hit-rate dashboards.
topics: Benchmarks to run and metrics to capture
next_steps: Liam to run end-to-end benchmark with canonicalized prompts (hashing) and report hit rate delta - Due 2025-02-24
Jared to share sample request traces and top-200 prompt variants by 2025-02-21
Maya to send updated caching recommendations doc and config snippet (TTL suggestions) by 2025-02-20
Schedule 1-hour deep-dive on personalization and cache partitioning w/ infra team - target 2025-02-27
action_items: Liam Chen - Run benchmark: TTL=60s vs TTL=300s, include KV/prefix hit rate and p99 latency - Due: 2025-02-24
Jared Brooks - Export 48h request traces and top prompt variants for personalization path - Due: 2025-02-21
Maya Patel - Share caching config snippets, suggested canonicalization library and example code - Due: 2025-02-20
Priya Singh - Identify 2 product flows to exclude from cache (security/personalization) and confirm - Due: 2025-02-22
transcript: [00:00] Maya Patel: Alright everyone, thanks for joining. This is the weekly POC caching sync for Aperture Labs. We got about 45 minutes on the calendar.
[00:12] Oliver Grant: Yep thanks Maya. I think today Jared has some updated numbers?

[00:18] Jared Brooks: Yeah I pulled the last 72 hours of KV and prefix cache stats. Overall hit rate for the general supply flow is about 62%, prefix cache hit rate sits at 48% and KV specific hits are about 55% but the personalization route is only 12% hit which is... quite low.
[00:40] Liam Chen: Mm hmm, ok. When you say personalization route, are those prompts with user-specific tokens, or are we seeing prompt style variants?

[00:46] Jared Brooks: Mostly both. There are a bunch of micro-variants
like names, dates, and some dynamic metadata embedded in the prompt template. So the fingerprinting isn't matching.
[01:05] Priya Singh: We suspected that. The front-end injects tracking IDs and session tokens in the prompt for auditability. We didn't want to strip those earlier because of debugging needs.

[01:22] Maya Patel: Right, that's a common tradeoff. For the POC our recommendation is to canonicalize prompts before caching
ship session IDs, normalize date formats, and hash the canonical string for KV keys. That usually lifts hit rates significantly.
[01:38] Jared Brooks: We tried a simple normalization last week, saw a bump to about 58% on the general flow, but didn't roll it across the personalization path yet.
[01:51] Liam Chen: Did that change impact tokenization or the outputs? Any quality regressions?
[01:56] Jared Brooks: Minimal from our quick manual checks; in a handful of cases the model output looked slightly less tailored, but accuracy on our red-team prompts was unchanged.

[02:09] Maya Patel: That's expected. Another lever is TTL
shorter TTLs reduce stale hits for personalization but also lowers effective hit rate. What TTLs are you using now?
[02:18] Jared Brooks: Default is 300s for most routes, 60s for high-frequency endpoints.
[02:23] Priya Singh: For personalization we set 60s as well, but because fingerprint variance is high we're still low.

[02:31] Liam Chen: Ok. Two parallel experiments I suggest: 1) canonicalization + hashing with current TTLs; 2) increase TTL for canonicalized keys to 300s to observe tradeoff. We'll measure hit rate, p50/p95 token latency, and cost per 1k requests.
[02:48] Oliver Grant: How does Redwood runtime handle prefix vs KV caching under the hood? Are those separate stores?

[02:55] Liam Chen: Good question. Prefix caching is more about reusing cached KV cache entries for repeated prefix tokens in the runtime
it's local to the serving node and tuned for latency. KV cache is a higher-level logical cache keyed on the prompt fingerprint and can be global. Both can be used together; we often canonicalize prompt then look up KV, and if missed we use partial prefix caching while generating.
[03:20] Jared Brooks: We saw a couple of spikes where the global KV store returned errors, and fallback to no-cache trips our cost dramatically. We captured logs around 03:00 UTC on Friday.
[03:30] Maya Patel: We should definitely look at those logs. Do you have trace IDs? That will help pin down if it was a transient capacity issue or a client-side miskeying.
[03:38] Jared Brooks: I do; I'll export the traces as part of the action items.

[03:45] Priya Singh: Another question
what's the behavior for personalized content that must not be cached for compliance? Can we partition caches or use tags to exclude keys?

[03:55] Liam Chen: Yes, we recommend using cache partitioning: add a tenant or policy flag in the key metadata. For sensitive flows, you can opt-out of KV but still use ephemeral prefix caching on the serving node and ensure logs don't persist user content. We also support TTL=0 for no caching.
[04:14] Oliver Grant: Curious about metrics: Jared, can you share the top N prompt templates by frequency? That might inform canonicalization rules.
[04:21] Jared Brooks: Yes, I have the top-200; I'll attach them in the CRM and in the Slack channel.

[04:28] Maya Patel: Great. For canonicalization, our suggested quick-win is a small transform: remove session IDs regex, normalize dates to ISO, collapse whitespace, lowercase non-proper nouns optionally. Liam can share a snippet.
[04:43] Liam Chen: I'll paste the code snippet after the call. It uses a deterministic hash (sha256) of the normalized prompt and optionally a namespace bit for product flow.

[04:51] Jared Brooks: One observation: after canonicalization we saw many prompts collapse into the same fingerprint but still some leakage because of free-text user inputs
like variable product descriptions.
[04:59] Priya Singh: Could we do partial matching? e.g., canonicalize functionally relevant parts and include a "payload" segment that's not hashed, then use combined lookup logic?

[05:09] Liam Chen: Yes, hybrid keys are an option: a stable prefix fingerprint and a small ephemeral payload. If prefix hits, runtime can warm KV for the payload or use prefix caching to speed up generation. That reduces cold-start token generation.

[05:27] Maya Patel: Let's be mindful of personalization quality
if payload influences intent heavily, caching could harm UX. So pick flows where the prompt structure is stable and payload is superficial.
[05:38] Oliver Grant: Right, like templated marketing copy vs. personal messages.

[05:42] Jared Brooks: Regarding hit-rate dashboards, I'll export the per-route hit rate, cache size, evictions, and p95 latency. There's a weird pattern where evictions spike around the daily traffic surge.

[05:55] Liam Chen: Evictions during surge may indicate small cache capacity or poor key locality. Increasing capacity or adjusting LRU policy could help. Also we can suggest candidate quantiles for eviction thresholds.

[06:08] Maya Patel: For the POC metrics, let's define success criteria: reach >75% KV/prefix combined hit rate on non-personalized flows, and >40% on personalization after canonicalization, without more than 5% delta in answer quality as judged by your test set.
[06:26] Priya Singh: That sounds reasonable. Timeline wise, if we run the canonicalization experiment this week we can reconvene next Wednesday.

[06:34] Maya Patel: Perfect. Action items recap: Liam runs benchmarks (TTL=60 vs 300 + canonicalization), Jared shares traces and top templates, Maya shares the config snippet. Priya to confirm excluded flows.

[06:47] Oliver Grant: One more thing
cost modeling. Can Redwood provide an estimate of token cost delta with increased hit rate?

[06:54] Maya Patel: Yes we can model that. Liam will include cost-per-1k-request estimates in the benchmark report; the console also has token-level cost breakdown per route which I'll export for you.
[07:06] Jared Brooks: I'll also flag any security-sensitive prompts that must be excluded from cache. There are about 8 endpoints that we think fall into that category.
[07:15] Liam Chen: For the benchmark we should capture: requests/sec distribution, prefix/KV hit rate, p50/p95 latency, token counts, and error/fallback rate.
[07:24] Priya Singh: Do you want us to provision a dedicated test pool for this or use hosted?

[07:29] Maya Patel: For reliability of results, Dedicated pools are ideal but not required for initial experiments. If you have Dedicated, point traffic there; otherwise we can tag these test routes in Hosted and isolate with a lower concurrency profile.
[07:42] Oliver Grant: We're on hosted for the POC so let's proceed there. We'll tag the test traffic and share the sampling keys.
[07:49] Maya Patel: Ok, final recap and I'll follow up with the notes and the canonicalization snippet. Any other questions?
[07:55] Jared Brooks: None from me, thanks everyone.
[08:00] Priya Singh: Thanks, talk soon.
[08:03] Maya Patel: Thanks all, see you next week.
